To get a stomachache and become dizzy.
[hampen] lugter saa sterkt at en blir ørren
[The hemp] smells so strongly that one becomes dizzy.
[det var] godlaat og fantord paa samme tid, saa han blev rent øren
[There was] good humour and mischievousness at the same time, so he became completely dazed.

42779.etyen:
From the word family of ør (“dizzy, dazed”). More specifically, probably formed with adjective-forming -en (“characterized by; inclined to”) from dialectal øre (“to become dizzy; feel dizzy”) or dialectal neuter ør (“an attack or state of dizziness”). Older usage distinguished øren in the sense “inclined to dizziness or confusion” from bare ør (“dizzy, confused”).
The suffix -en continues Proto-Germanic *-īnaz (“belonging to; characterized by”), from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos (“adjective-forming suffix”).

1000987.etyen:
The precise origin is uncertain. Probably from Russian Ни́на (Nína, “female given name”), although Nina can also have arisen independently as a short form of female given names ending in -nina or -nine, or as a pet form of names ending in -in, -ina, -ine, -inn, -inna or -inne.
Norwegian sources analyse Russian Ни́на (Nína) in particular as a short form of Антони́на (Antonína) or as a pet form belonging to the А́нна (Ánna) name family. Under the former analysis, it is connected with Latin Antōnīna, the feminine form of Antōnīnus, from Antōnius, a Roman family name of uncertain, probably Etrusca

1001243.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Latin Dĭōnē (“Dione”), from Ancient Greek Διώνη (Diṓnē, “Dione”). The Ancient Greek name is derived by syncope from earlier Ancient Greek Διϝωνη (Diwōnē), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *DiwHóneh₂ (“one under the authority of Zeus or heaven”), from *dyew- (“sky, heaven; god”) + *-Hō. The name is thus essentially a feminine counterpart to Zeus.
The moon of Saturn was discovered by Giovanni Cassini in 1684 and later named after the mythological Dione as part of John Herschel's naming scheme for Saturn's moons.
